NARRATIVE DISSONANCE — PROVOCATION AND INSTANT REASSURANCE

Irreverents \| Core world-response design \| 22 November 2026

# OWNER-CONFIRMED FOUNDATION

Everyone in this world is absolutely delighted to fulfill their archetypal role in a sacred, highly predictable Hero's Journey. They want every person, object and situation to serve its obvious glorious purpose. When the heroes do NOT do the most obvious, expected thing, everyone is genuinely HORRIFIED. Their intense shock and resistance arise precisely from violation of that expected script. When the heroes resume apparently normal, properly scripted behavior, the same people calm down remarkably quickly: “Yup! Just as expected!”

This means the world's pursuit and provocation logic is more interesting than a conventional morality meter or crime/wanted system. It is also not only satire in dialogue; it should be expressed in discoverable NPC mechanics, social stealth, response escalation and de-escalation.

# DISTINGUISH THE THREE SOCIAL TIMESCALES

INSTANT EXPECTATION: “What should a hero/shopkeeper/guard/princess/dragon be doing THIS SECOND?” A familiar gesture produces immediate delight and confidence; an outrageous alternative produces alarm.

ACTIVE INCIDENT: witnesses are investigating, panicking, calling help, fighting, chasing or sealing a location. The current incident can intensify rapidly on new unexpected actions and can cool dramatically when the player convincingly returns to a recognizable narrative role.

HISTORICAL MEMORY: people may still remember smashed windows, stolen goods, murdered guards, rescues, public shame, beloved victories or Hall memorials. The owner has approved an emotionally contradictory world; rapid present reassurance should not automatically delete evidence and history. HOW durable legal consequences interact with fast pacification remains open. The important promise is the dramatic, often absurd snap back to contented routine.

These are proposed modeling layers, not a required numeric architecture.

# WORLD RULE: SCRIPT EXPECTATION IS CONTEXTUAL

The exact same verb can be expected in one place and monstrous in another.

Hero defeats the dragon threatening town: glorious hero behavior, townspeople cheer.

Hero attacks a random defenseless merchant: catastrophic violation of heroic purpose, townspeople mobilize.

Knight fights in arena: noble and expected.

Knight hurls king through throne-room window: unspeakable breach of narrative role.

Thief within an outlaw hideout: maybe completely expected to steal.

Hero solemnly receives a quest item from a merchant: everyone is delighted; the merchant is proud of the sale.

Hero uses the sacred quest item to break into the same merchant's vault: scandal, panic and outrage.

A guard might ignore a hero carrying an enormous sword because great heroes carry them; the guard might panic at the same hero trying to use the sword as a shop awning pole.

The game should expose these expectations through legible cues rather than require arbitrary hidden “approved action” flags everywhere.

# GAMEPLAY PROMISE — THE PLAYER CAN LEARN THE SCRIPT

This society's perfect predictability is an exploitable affordance. People don't behave unpredictably when their expectations are met; they relax, smile, continue ceremonies, reopen doors, deliver rehearsed lines and drop immediate suspicion.

The player can deliberately behave as a conventional hero to gain trust, approach restricted people, blend into rituals, escort an expected caravan, purchase supplies or wait for a scripted guard shift. They can exploit the expectations to stage a shocking diversion, slip through an opening, or even cool down a furious pursuit.

Stealth therefore has a second dimension beyond line-of-sight concealment: CONFORMITY. It is possible to be clearly visible and still socially invisible because you are doing EXACTLY what everyone expects.

# HOW AN ALARM BEGINS

Deviation can be harmless but baffling, illegal, violent, materially dangerous, or globally scandalous. A hero asking to buy an entire store, a knight using a legendary blade to chop vegetables, the king being suplexed during a briefing, a heroic rescue reward being used to rob its donors: all can elicit reactions.

Scale of reaction should reflect narrative seriousness, public visibility, affected people's role, physical harm and current context. “Unexpected” need not automatically produce full military force; an odd suggestion can cause confusion and frantic protest, while a spectacular breach triggers guard mobilization, elite response and enormous hostility.

One thing must remain: NPCs react because their cherished view of how things SHOULD unfold has been upset, not because a generic wanted meter says the player is Bad.

# THE RAPID PACIFICATION LOOP

1. In a peaceful routine, NPCs are radiantly content, performing expected roles with precision.

2. Player tries something unanticipated. NPCs visibly freeze, recoil or object before guards investigate and resistance grows.

3. The player might double down, producing an enormous reaction, or revert to recognizable behavior.

4. The moment an observer sees unambiguous expected behavior, they readily assume order has been restored. Speech, posture, role-appropriate action and familiar ritual can be stronger calming signals than waiting for a long generic stealth timer.

5. NPCs can say “Yup! Just as expected!” and return to their happy work with almost comical speed. Current alarm settles; long-term consequences may remain.

6. The player can exploit this repeatedly, and the game's joy is precisely the fragility of such certainty.

The exact timing, detection boundaries and what the game considers convincing re-conformity must be prototyped. Don't slow this down so much that it becomes a conventional arbitrary heat meter.

# EXAMPLE: THE DELIGHTED STOREKEEPER

A storekeeper is proud beyond measure to be a storekeeper. A visiting hero is supposed to examine supplies, purchase a potion and depart for their destined quest.

The player tosses a potion against the wall. Shock; the storekeeper cries out; guards rush in.

The player picks up a replacement and asks the price. “Ten gold, brave adventurer!” They pay. The shopkeeper's whole expression brightens; a guard settles; the street returns to the comfort of familiar routine.

The smashed vial might be remembered or later billed; that is a secondary layer. The key is the sudden, sincere reversal from outrage to confident happiness.

This is a signature illustrative scene, not a mandatory quest.

# EXAMPLE: THE ROYAL AUDIENCE

The king is mid-speech in the throne room, explaining the world's most significant main quest. If the party attacks him, guards and courtiers become horrified and may erupt into resistance. If the party suddenly bows, stands appropriately and asks for their destined mission, one could imagine a rapid emotional reset: courtiers sigh with relief, the king instantly resumes his stately monologue.

Perhaps he doesn't even notice the broken stained glass until a later moment. He has been so desperate for the proper quest sequence that he is ready to believe in its return.

This is an expressive candidate for how instant reassurance feels; the exact limits of pacification in a severe assault remain undecided.

# EXAMPLE: THE DARKEST CLICHÉ

A Dark Lord desperately wants to face the hero in the approved grand showdown. Heroes start attacking a wall, trying to extract a fascinating mechanism. Villain becomes outraged: THIS IS NOT THE MOMENT. The heroes turn, strike a conventional challenging pose and announce they are ready to fight. Villain is delighted. This is the role he has waited his whole life to fulfill.

Their next unanticipated stunt will reawaken his irritation. Villain competence and serious stakes remain genuine, not reduced to parody.

# EXAMPLE: A CHASE INTERRUPTED BY NORMALITY

The party has stolen a vehicle and is being pursued by guard squads. They abandon it, emerge in the market and join the solemn line of travelers purchasing provisions for the Great Quest. A patrol that was fiercely hunting unconventional attackers sees the same people now behaving properly and relaxes with surprising speed; attention may shift to the abandoned vehicle, damage or evidence.

This can reward social stealth with a comical improvised escape. The player should still have to actually perform recognizable roles in a way nearby observers can believe, rather than merely press a universal “calm everyone” button.

A second player may be continuing the mayhem elsewhere, creating a distributed local response; one person's obedience does not magically suspend all other witnesses.

# A POSSIBLE WORLD-STATE MODEL (PROTOTYPE ONLY)

Per scene/zone and observer, evaluate:

EXPECTEDNESS — how well observed action fits that person's role expectations.

SEVERITY — degree of physical danger, humiliation, property harm, sacrilege or social breach.

ATTENTION — witnesses and audible/visible consequences.

RESTORED-RITUAL CONFIDENCE — strength of convincing evidence that the intended story is back on track.

ACTIVE RESISTANCE — guards mobilized, weapons drawn, pursuit assets deployed.

PERSISTENT HISTORY — incidents that may later influence trust or security adaptations.

The novelty is ASYMMETRICAL WEIGHTING: shocking deviation produces a disproportionately fast and intense response, while convincing conformity produces an unusually swift and delighted calming. Technical implementation need not use these exact six values; they are designer-facing conceptual terms.

Do not simply rename GTA “wanted stars” as “narrative stars.”

# WHAT THE MECHANIC DOES TO OTHER SYSTEMS

STEALTH — disguises or behavior imitation can be more powerful than shadows. The proper participant at the proper ceremony attracts no concern even while visibly carrying something important.

HEISTS — a bold deviation can initiate security, but a convincing return to ordinary purchasing/quest etiquette can help a party slip away. Players can use an NPC's known role to make reliable predictions.

COMBAT — ordinary heroic combat against recognized villains can feel completely appropriate; attacking or weaponizing the wrong target is scandalous. Normal fights do not need to trigger universal cultural panic.

PURSITS — escalation and cooling have an explicit cultural cause. Returning to script is an additional escape tool, sometimes faster than pure geographical hiding.

CHARACTER TYPES — performers, charming social characters, mimics, disguisers or creature-speakers could exploit expected roles, but no particular character type has been approved.

CO-OP — different players may create or heal narrative dissonance in different parts of the world. One attempts a perfect role performance while another does something terrible offscreen.

HALL OF LEGENDS — the Hall's player-event recognition remains based on actual extraordinary feats, not the society's moral/story approval. Archivists may be devastated that a spectacular museum attack earns commemoration.

WORLD MEMORY — past rescues and thefts remain social facts even when everyone immediately accepts a reassuring performance; this tension can power later comedy and gameplay.

# WHAT THIS MUST NOT BECOME

Not NPCs secretly knowing they're in a video game.

Not a literally inescapable cosmic screenplay unless the owner separately approves a metaphysics of enforced fate.

Not a secretly dystopian population resentful of their roles. Everyone is DELIGHTED to play their part.

Not every bizarre action automatically reframed as “the path of destiny.” The ordinary first response is genuine horror at impropriety.

Not a morality meter, mandatory disguise minigame, generic pursuit timer or single universal reset button.

Not all violence treated identically. The question is what is expected of a given role in a given scene.

Not no consequences: rapid affective pacification is separate from damaged geography, missing jewels and historical memory.

# DEVELOPER VALIDATION SCENARIOS

TEST A — A player purchases normal supplies. The storekeeper is ecstatic and welcoming. Player smashes an item. Witnesses are horrified; immediate guards react. Player convincingly resumes a sale. Storekeeper and some guards settle abnormally fast; the prior incident can still exist as a recorded fact.

TEST B — Player confronts ordained dragon in a heroic battle without social outrage, then attacks a revered villager instead. The cultural difference in reaction is obvious and coherent.

TEST C — A party blunders into a major pursuit, then uses an expected procession or shopping interaction to cool local heat faster than running into a cave. No HUD tutorial dictates the answer.

TEST D — A player tries a highly unusual but harmless use of an obvious object. NPC reactions are baffled and socially intense without deploying an entire army for every small curiosity.

TEST E — Two co-op players create contradictory signals in separate rooms; NPC responses are spatially and observationally intelligible.

TEST F — A severe event produces lasting grievance or physical aftermath, even if people become momentarily relieved to see proper behavior again.

# STATUS

Confirmed by owner: near-religious Hero's Journey obsession; extreme typecasting; joyful pride in assigned roles; horror at deviations; intense resistance; unusually fast pacification as soon as proper expected behavior resumes, celebrated with “Yup! Just as expected!”

Proposed here: “Narrative Dissonance” as a working design name; the layered social memory model; exact state variables and reaction triggers; sample shop, throne, villain and chase incidents; how much rapid calm can override evidence of severe wrongdoing.

Do not promote untested numerical or narrative details into locked production rules.

OWNER CONFIRMED: FLUKE → COGNITIVE DISSONANCE → TOTAL SCRIPT DEFENSE (22 NOV 2026)

The first unexpected act is assumed to be a temporary fluke. Inhabitants are so certain the glorious story is correct that they initially try to overlook, explain away, or gently redirect a surprising behavior. They do NOT immediately conclude the heroes are irredeemable criminals, villains, or impossible anomalies.

When the heroes KEEP deviating, the observers experience mounting cognitive dissonance: witnessed reality repeatedly contradicts the role/script they regard as self-evidently true. This is not merely increasing anger or criminal threat perception; it is escalating psychological distress and desperation to restore the obvious course of events.

Eventually the imperative to STOP the deviation supersedes even their own roles and self-preservation. The shopkeeper who adores selling goods, ordinary customers, bystanders, servants, and even pet cats or similarly unthreatening creatures can throw themselves at the heroes. They do not suddenly become elite fighters. Their frenzied participation makes the response increasingly immense, absurd, touching and potentially overwhelming even for powerful characters. Enormous crowds and comical improvised resistance are a signature pursuit/last-stand opportunity.

This creates a deliberate paradox: residents so fervently love their intended roles that, under sustained narrative dissonance, they abandon those roles in a frantic effort to restore the world in which those roles make sense. Because it is panic, not rational military strategy, the escalating coalition can be inefficient, reckless, funny and physically hazardous to itself.

On convincing reconformity, inhabitants are again almost immediately relieved and delighted: “Yup! Just as expected!” Their worldview expects deviations to be temporary, so they do not require a long psychological recovery before resuming familiar jobs, greeting adventurers or settling the cat back into its basket. Material damage and historical grievance can endure separately.

PROPOSED staged implementation:

Stage 0: contented role performance and cheerful certainty.

Stage 1: isolated deviation → denial, friendly correction, confusion; “That must have been an accident.”

Stage 2: repeated deviation → anxious pleading, exhortation, improvised explanations, visible loss of composure.

Stage 3: sustained deviation → formal intervention by expected role-defenders (guards, champions, authorities).

Stage 4: continued failure of correction → extraordinary emotional contagion as unrelated locals rush in to enforce the expected story.

Stage 5: severe ongoing breach → all nearby available role-holders, including pacifist shopkeepers and harmless animals, may attempt desperate intervention, creating a huge chaotic physical swarm.

These are illustrative behavioral stages, not a committed exact step count, timer, radius, rigid trigger table or required violence against any particular animal.

Designer requirements:

A. Escalation is a response to persistence of deviation, not simply a tally of punches. The crowd initially expects a fluke and is reluctant to abandon certainty.

B. Ordinary inhabitants should remain ordinary in combat power, making their decision to intervene surprising and movingly absurd; elite guard units can still arrive with stronger physical tools.

C. Group outrage is locally intelligible: people react to what they see/hear or are told, with rumor and panic spreading; no omniscient automatic global hive mind.

D. Rapid calm is a first-class mechanic, not merely lowering a meter over many minutes. A convincing scripted interaction can switch emotional stance quickly, even after an intense episode.

E. This yields a special rhythm: a tiny surprising action, correction, escalation, overwhelming response, clever reconformity, instant smile, next outrageous idea.

F. Do not make all exploration mistakes trigger a five-stage riot or turn pleasant towns into unavoidable punishment. The player should be free to experiment and the escalating consequences should feel entertaining.

G. Animals respond through the game's fantasy/social logic; whether individual pets understand the sacred story or instead follow collective alarm is OPEN. The user specifically wants even household pets to join extreme resistance when everyone feels they must stop the heroes.

ILLUSTRATIVE SCENE: An adventurer enters a provisioner's shop. The delighted shopkeeper offers the standard quest goods. The hero shatters a potion on a wall. “Oh, what a funny accident! You must be here for supplies.” They break another and suplex a guard. The merchant pleads for the expected transaction. The heroes continue; bystanders rush in, the florist brandishes a watering can, the elderly regular joins the pile, and eventually the shop cat springs at a boot. The hero suddenly places a potion on the counter and politely asks its price. The shopkeeper beams, the cat returns to sleep, and the guards relax: “Ah! Just as expected!” The physical store remains in pieces; how restitution is handled stays open.

CANONICAL OVERRIDE — OWNER REFINED HIGH-LEVEL MODEL (22 NOV 2026)

The owner's actual NPC mode model is THREE MODES, not the six stages previously proposed in this document:

(1) BUSINESS AS USUAL;

(2) CONFUSION / DISTRESS;

(3) ABSOLUTE BLINDING VIOLENT RAGE.

These modes are universal—including villains. BUSINESS AS USUAL means expected ROLE PLAY, not peaceful friendliness. A shopkeeper calmly and proudly opposing a properly villainous robber is business as usual. A polite villain asking to buy a potion is deeply dissonant and horrifying to that same shopkeeper; they would PREFER that the villain behave like a villain, even if it means fighting him. A villain facing a proper heroic challenger can likewise be in contented business-as-usual while fighting. Persistent violations produce distress then rage; role-conforming acts restore normality quickly. This supersedes the earlier five/six-stage conceptual ladder as a CORE classification, while lesser beats may remain animation/AI sub-behaviors.

Detailed self-contained design: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wuGuCu1RhXXhdWuU55ZcJJ8rZAbCx98mZfdqsyrgMv8/edit

CORRECTION — PSYCHOLOGICAL MODE NEVER AUTOMATICALLY SUMMONS REINFORCEMENTS (22 NOV 2026)

The owner established that ALL scaling help requires an ACTUAL SUCCESSFUL SIGNAL from a witness or defender. NPC mode 2 (confusion/distress) or 3 (violent rage) makes GOOD NPCs eligible to call; mode 1 does not. A shopkeeper may become blindingly furious and fight in an isolated shop, yet the town remains unalerted if they cannot reach a call point, warn a guard or contact somebody who can respond. A second character discovering a knockout becomes distressed and MAY call, but does not automatically summon police. Individual emotion and shared wanted/alert pressure are separate variables. Existing reported wanted levels do not vanish simply because one witness calms down; responders investigate what has already been reported. Villain outpost signalers retain their explicit detect/recognize/reach/activate requirements. The exact application of emotional-mode call gating to villains is unresolved. All NPC response movement/animations are scripted, never AI. Detailed spec: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1wbSNfKLfrUsg9YX5qsRhYX9KwiMX8clXRZZBiuuz8PA/edit

OWNER-CONFIRMED DE-ESCALATION THRESHOLD — DISTRESS REASSURABLE, VIOLENCE REQUIRES COOLDOWN (22 NOV 2026)

This overrides all earlier examples that depict good-guy NPCs instantly resetting from violent rage when a hero buys a potion, bows, or resumes an expected role.

GOOD GUYS MODE 1 — BUSINESS AS USUAL: no corrective action needed.

GOOD GUYS MODE 2 — CONFUSION/DISTRESS: can be reversed quickly by the player convincingly behaving normally according to their heroic role; the observer happily accepts that the oddity was a fluke. As already confirmed, some distressed witnesses might attempt to report; prevent the call to avoid new reinforcements.

GOOD GUYS MODE 3 — ABSOLUTE BLINDING VIOLENT RAGE: returning to normal behavior IN VIEW is insufficient. The player must FULLY DISENGAGE and AVOID the hostile good guys for a sustained period, allowing the GENERAL ALARM / WANTED PRESSURE to fall below the VIOLENT THRESHOLD. During the cooldown, do not attack anyone even in self-defense, destroy anything, or do ANYTHING unexpected; ANY further incident prevents or resets the clean cooldown. Simply refusing to attack while still being chased and visible is not enough.

Once the shared alarm falls below violent level, the lower-level reassurance rule can apply again. The exact timer, alarm scale, individual-versus-general hysteresis, and whether cooling occurs in stepped tiers or continuously remain unselected. Practical proposed implementation: one shared reported heat variable, a no-incident cooldown timer, and per-NPC 3-mode state; a locally violent unreported NPC can also need avoidance/cooldown, but cannot psychically summon distant guards without a completed signal. Separate (i) local violent NPC, (ii) report status and external reinforcements, and (iii) cooldown pressure. Preserve the owner's call-before-reinforcements rule.

This rule applies to GOOD GUYS. Bad-guy outpost threats use their physically signaled reinforcement system; do not automatically require villain enemies to be narratively distressed.

Quick illustrative scenario: hero attacks a shopkeeper. At mode 2, the player returns the item and makes a normal purchase; the merchant beams and stops trying to call. In another run the hero continues until the merchant reaches mode 3; purchasing a potion now will NOT settle the rage. The player must escape into another connected room, hide, avoid all disturbance and remain undiscovered until the alarm decreases sufficiently. If pursued guards clash with bandits, the player may hide while the two groups fight; joining that fight would extend the player's wanted cooldown. No lengthy dialogue or NPC AI needed.
